title: An autonomous feedback protocol: responding to temperature and potential changes in energy converters
authors: Krishna Lyn Delima, Elsa Danielsson, Bruno Bertin-Johannet, Janine Splettstoesser
abstract: Nanoscale thermoelectric devices convert tiny amounts of heat into power. But what happens if the external conditions and resulting temperature differences are not a priori known? We propose a feedback mechanism that optimizes the performance of a quantum-point-contact-based heat engine (QPC). A quantum-dot detector measures the external conditions and gives autonomous feedback on the QPC's properties. We expect this feedback mechanism to be experimentally relevant for steady-state engines with unknown external conditions and for adapting dynamic charging processes to the potential buildup.
summary: This work proposes an autonomous feedback control protocol for quantum heat engines using a coupled quantum dot detector. By using the QD to sense external temperature and potential changes, the system dynamically adjusts its energy filter to maximize power output or charging voltage. This demonstrates how feedback can significantly improve energy conversion efficiency under realistic, fluctuating operating conditions.
main_problem: The paper develops and analyzes an autonomous feedback protocol to optimize the performance of quantum-point-contact-based heat engines when external temperature and potential conditions are unknown or variable.
main_result: Feedback mechanisms significantly enhance energy conversion, allowing the device to optimize power output across varying temperature distributions or increase the charging voltage in open-circuit battery setups.
method: The analysis combines coherent steady-state transport theory for the QPC with stochastic rate equations for the coupled quantum dot detector, optimizing parameters based on probability distributions.
model_or_system: The system is a quantum-point-contact (QPC) heat engine coupled to a quantum dot (QD) detector. The QD reads out the electrochemical potential ($\mu_c$) to autonomously adjust the QPC's energy filter, thereby controlling the thermoelectric energy conversion.
key_observables: Charge current ($I$), average output power ($ ar{P}$), final charging potential ($\mu_c$), and the QD occupation probabilities ($p_e, p_f$).
important_parameters: Temperature bias ($	ext{Th}, 	ext{Tc}$), capacitive coupling strength ($U$), and the rates governing QD tunneling ($\Gamma_{ef}, \Gamma_{fe}$).
main_assumptions: Assumptions include mean-field descriptions for electron interactions, fast electron traversal compared to QD dynamics, and the QD coupling only to the cold contact.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison of voltage build-up (battery setup) and power output (load setup) with and without feedback under varying temperature conditions (Normal, Uniform, Bimodal distributions).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the basic feedback mechanism in steady-state (load setup) to analyzing charging dynamics (battery setup), then extending the analysis to optimize performance under unknown, time-varying temperature distributions using probability theory.
why_interesting: The combination of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, stochastic processes (QD dynamics), and optimization techniques for energy harvesting makes it highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems operating under fluctuating external parameters.
